Inventing a Recommender System

How does Netflix know what you should watch next? How does Spotify build your Discover Weekly? Nobody at those companies watches movies on your behalf and takes notes. The trick is beautifully simple:

Find people whose taste matches yours, and recommend what they loved and you haven't seen yet.

This is called collaborative filtering, and in this chapter you will invent it from scratch -- using real movie ratings collected from a live class of students. By the end you will compute, for any person in the class, the three movies they are most likely to enjoy.

The plan:

  1. Clean the data -- real data is messy: missing ratings, people who barely rated anything, generous vs stingy raters.
  2. Measure taste similarity -- invent cosine similarity, then compute every pair of similarities in a single matrix multiplication.
  3. Recommend -- combine similarity with ratings to score unseen movies.
  4. Bonus -- how would this scale to Netflix size? Invent the MapReduce trick for multiplying gigantic sparse matrices.

You'll need pandas and numpy. If you know a little pandas (reading a CSV, selecting columns) you're ready; we'll introduce everything else as we go.

Part 1: The Data

Run the cell below as-is. It loads movies_ratings.csv -- 25 Bollywood movies rated 0-5 by 18 people (a real class!). Rows are movies, columns are people, and an empty cell means that person never rated that movie. Pandas shows these as NaN (Not a Number -- pandas' way of saying "no data here").

Load the Data

Run the cell below as-is to load the dataset.

Part 2: Cleaning Real Data

Drop People Who Barely Rated Anything

Look at the data: the table is full of NaN. Some people rated almost every movie; a few rated nothing at all. Someone with 0 or 2 ratings tells us nothing about their taste -- keeping them would only add noise.

Your task: build a DataFrame called ratings that keeps only the people (columns) who rated at least 3 movies.

Hint 1

You need to count how many non-NaN values each column has. The method .count() on a DataFrame does exactly this -- it counts real (non-missing) values per column.

Hint 2

Use boolean indexing on columns: raw.loc[:, raw.count() >= 3] keeps only the columns (people) where the count of real ratings is 3 or more.

Solution 
ratings = raw.loc[:, raw.count() >= 3]

Generous Raters vs Stingy Raters

Print ratings.mean().sort_values(). Notice something? Bhaskar's average rating is about 1.7 while Venu's is about 4.1. Does Venu love every movie and Bhaskar hate them all? More likely they just use the scale differently -- a 3 from Bhaskar might mean the same as a 5 from Venu.

If we compare raw numbers, the stingy and generous raters will look like they disagree even when their taste is identical. We need to put everyone on the same scale.

The fix -- min-max scaling, per person: You derived a normalization formula in the Loops & Arrays chapter that maps any value to the range [0, 1] using the minimum and maximum. The formula is: (value - min) / (max - min). Apply that same idea here, column by column, so each person's lowest rating becomes 0 and highest becomes 1.

Your task: create scaled from ratings using that formula, applied column-by-column.

Hint 1

In pandas, ratings.min() and ratings.max() compute the minimum and maximum per column by default. When you subtract or divide a row-vector from a DataFrame, pandas applies the operation to every row automatically.

Hint 2

Plug the three pandas calls into the formula: (ratings - ratings.min()) / (ratings.max() - ratings.min()).

Solution 
scaled = (ratings - ratings.min()) / (ratings.max() - ratings.min())

Filling the Holes

The similarity math coming in Part 3 can't handle NaN -- we need a number in every cell. But which number?

Think about the options before reading on:

  • Fill with 0? That says "this person would hate this movie" -- a strong claim we have no evidence for.
  • Fill with 1? Same problem, opposite direction.
  • Fill with that person's average scaled rating? That says "no opinion -- assume they'd feel about it the way they feel about a typical movie." Neutral. This is the one.

Your task: create filled from scaled, replacing each NaN with the mean of that person's column.

Hint 1

The pandas method .fillna(value) replaces every NaN with the given value. If you pass a Series (one value per column), each column's NaNs get filled with that column's value.

Hint 2

scaled.mean() returns a Series of column means. Pass it directly: scaled.fillna(scaled.mean()).

Solution 
filled = scaled.fillna(scaled.mean())

Quick Check -- Why Normalize Ratings?

Before computing cosine similarity, you applied min-max scaling to each person's ratings. Why is this normalization step important?

A. It makes the computation faster

B. Without normalization, a generous rater (who gives 4s and 5s to everything) would appear similar to another generous rater even if their actual preferences are completely different

C. Python requires values between 0 and 1 for cosine similarity

D. It removes missing values from the matrix

Answer: B. Without normalization, people who rate on a similar scale look alike regardless of their actual tastes. Min-max scaling strips away the scale and keeps only the pattern of preferences.

Part 3: Measuring Taste

How Similar Are Two People?

Each person is now a column of 25 numbers -- a vector (just a list of numbers, one per movie).

Two people with similar taste should have vectors pointing in a similar direction. You already know the dot product from the Secrets of Prediction chapter. Think about these questions:

  • The dot product of two identical vectors is large. The dot product of vectors pointing in completely different directions (at right angles) is 0. So the dot product tells you something about alignment. But it also depends on how big the numbers are -- how can you remove that size effect?
  • What if you divided the dot product by both vectors' lengths? What would that give you for identical vectors? For vectors at right angles?

This quantity -- the dot product divided by the product of lengths -- is called cosine similarity: 1 means identical taste, 0 means completely unrelated taste. It measures direction only, which is one more defense against scale differences between raters.

Your task: write similarity(a, b) for two columns of filled.

Hint 1

The dot product of arrays a and b is np.dot(a, b) or equivalently (a * b).sum(). The length (magnitude) of a vector is np.linalg.norm(a) or np.sqrt((a**2).sum()).

Hint 2

Cosine similarity = dot(a, b) / (length(a) * length(b)). Return this single number.

Solution 
def similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

Unit Vectors

We want the similarity between every pair of people -- that's $15 \times 15 = 225$ numbers. Calling similarity in a double loop would work, but there is a spectacular shortcut. It starts with one observation:

What happens to the similarity formula when both vectors already have length 1? Simplify the formula and see what's left.

A vector divided by its own length has length 1 (called a unit vector). When both vectors are unit vectors, the denominator is $1 \times 1 = 1$, so cosine similarity becomes just the dot product.

Your task: build the numpy array uM where every column of M = filled.values is scaled to length 1.

Hint 1

The length of each column is np.sqrt((M**2).sum(axis=0)). Dividing each column by its length turns it into a unit vector.

Hint 2

uM = M / np.sqrt((M**2).sum(axis=0)) -- NumPy automatically applies the division to every row.

Solution 
M = filled.values
uM = M / np.sqrt((M**2).sum(axis=0))

All 225 Similarities at Once

Here's the payoff. Remember how matrix multiplication works: entry $(i, j)$ of the result $AB$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$.

So what is $uM^T \cdot uM$ (the transpose of uM times uM)? Row $i$ of $uM^T$ is column $i$ of $uM$ -- that's person $i$'s unit vector. So entry $(i, j)$ is the dot product of person $i$'s unit vector with person $j$'s unit vector... which is exactly their cosine similarity. One operation computes the entire similarity table. This is not a toy trick -- it is exactly how real recommender systems compute all-pairs similarity. (The same idea also appears inside the attention layers of large language models like ChatGPT, where every word computes its similarity to every other word.)

Your task: compute S = uM.T @ uM, then wrap it as a labeled DataFrame:

sim = pd.DataFrame(S, index=filled.columns, columns=filled.columns)

Before running the tests, predict: what should the diagonal of S be, and why? Should S equal its own transpose?

Hint 1

The diagonal entry (i, i) is the dot product of person i's unit vector with itself. The dot product of any unit vector with itself is 1. And since similarity(i, j) = similarity(j, i), the matrix is symmetric -- so yes, S equals its transpose.

Solution 
S = uM.T @ uM
sim = pd.DataFrame(S, index=filled.columns, columns=filled.columns)

Your Taste Twin

Your task: write most_similar(person) returning the name of the person with the highest similarity to person -- excluding the person themselves (everyone's best match would otherwise be themselves, similarity 1.0).

Hint 1

Look at sim[person] to see all similarity scores for that person. You need to skip the person's own entry before finding the maximum.

Hint 2

sim[person].drop(person).idxmax() removes the person's own entry and returns the name of whoever has the highest remaining similarity.

Solution 
def most_similar(person):
    return sim[person].drop(person).idxmax()

Quick Check -- The Matrix Multiplication Shortcut

You computed all 225 pairwise similarities with a single line: S = uM.T @ uM. Why did you need to convert each person's column to a unit vector before multiplying?

A. Python can only multiply matrices whose columns have length 1

B. Without unit vectors, the matrix product gives plain dot products, which depend on vector size -- not just the direction of taste. Unit vectors make every dot product equal to cosine similarity.

C. Unit vectors make the matrix smaller and use less memory

D. It doesn't matter -- the results would be the same without unit vectors

Answer: B. Cosine similarity is "dot product divided by both lengths." When both vectors already have length 1, the division disappears and the dot product is the cosine similarity. That's what makes the one-line matrix multiplication work.

Part 4: Making Recommendations

What Haven't You Seen?

We only want to recommend movies the person hasn't rated yet -- no point suggesting a movie they already gave 5 stars.

Careful: which table remembers what was actually rated? Not filled -- we erased that information when we filled the NaNs. Go back to ratings.

Your task: write unrated_movies(person) returning a list of movie names the person never rated.

Hint 1

Look at the person's column in ratings. The NaN entries are the movies they never rated. Use .isna() to find them.

Hint 2

ratings[person] gives the column. ratings[person].isna() gives True/False per movie. Use that boolean mask on ratings.index to get the movie names.

Solution 
def unrated_movies(person):
    return ratings.index[ratings[person].isna()].tolist()

The Recommender

Now assemble the pieces. To score a movie $m$ that person $p$ hasn't seen:

$$\text{score}(m, p) = \sum_{\text{person } q} \text{rating}(m, q) \cdot \text{sim}(p, q)$$

In plain English: everyone in the class votes with their (filled, scaled) rating of $m$, but people whose taste matches $p$'s get a louder voice. A movie loved by your taste twins scores high; a movie loved only by people you disagree with scores low.

Look closely -- that sum is a dot product: the movie's row of filled dotted with $p$'s column of sim. So all candidate scores at once is:

scores = filled.loc[candidates] @ sim[person]

Your task: write recommend(person, k=3) that scores every unrated movie and returns the k movie names with the highest scores, best first.

Hint 1

First, get the list of candidates with unrated_movies(person). Then compute scores using the one-liner above.

Hint 2

Sort the scores in descending order and take the top k: scores.sort_values(ascending=False).head(k).index.tolist().

Solution 
def recommend(person, k=3):
    candidates = unrated_movies(person)
    scores = filled.loc[candidates] @ sim[person]
    return scores.sort_values(ascending=False).head(k).index.tolist()

Quick Check -- The Cold Start Problem

A brand-new user signs up and hasn't rated any movies yet. What happens when the recommender tries to find their taste twin?

A. The system recommends the most popular movies by default

B. Cosine similarity can't be computed -- the user's rating vector is all zeros (or NaN), so there's no direction to compare

C. The system assigns random ratings and proceeds normally

D. The user is automatically matched with the most active rater

Answer: B. With no ratings, the user's vector is all zeros or all NaN. A zero vector has no direction, so cosine similarity is undefined (you'd be dividing by zero). This is the famous cold-start problem -- it's why every streaming service asks new users to "pick a few titles you like" before showing recommendations.

You just built a working collaborative-filtering recommender on real data. Try recommend(...) on a few more people -- do the suggestions make sense given who their taste twin is?

One honest limitation to notice: what would recommend("YouJustJoined") do for a brand-new person with zero ratings? Nothing useful -- there's no vector to compare. This is the famous cold-start problem, and it's why every streaming service pesters new users to "pick a few titles you like" before showing recommendations.

Part 5: Two More Recommender Moves

Ask Your Five Best Taste Twins

recommend() let everyone vote, weighted by similarity. Real systems often do something simpler and cheaper: find your top 5 most similar people, pool their top 5 favorite movies, and drop anything you've already seen. No scores, no weighted sums -- just "what do people like me love?"

Your task: write three functions:

  • top5_similar_people(person) -- the 5 most similar people (by sim, excluding the person), most similar first.
  • top5_favorites(person) -- the person's 5 highest-rated movies. Use ratings (their real opinions), and .dropna() before sorting.
  • recommend_by_friends(person) -- pool the friends' favorites in order, remove movies person has already rated, and drop duplicates while keeping first appearance.

Then compare with recommend(person, 3) from Part 4 -- do the two strategies agree?

Hint 1

For top5_similar_people: use sim[person].drop(person).nlargest(5).index.tolist().

Hint 2

For top5_favorites: use ratings[person].dropna().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).index.tolist().

Hint 3

For recommend_by_friends: loop through the friends from top5_similar_people, collect their favorites, filter out movies the person already rated, and use dict.fromkeys(pool).keys() or pandas .drop_duplicates() to remove duplicates while keeping order.

Solution 
def top5_similar_people(person):
    return sim[person].drop(person).nlargest(5).index.tolist()

def top5_favorites(person):
    return ratings[person].dropna().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).index.tolist()

def recommend_by_friends(person):
    rated = set(ratings.index[ratings[person].notna()])
    pool = []
    for friend in top5_similar_people(person):
        pool.extend(top5_favorites(friend))
    seen = set()
    result = []
    for m in pool:
        if m not in rated and m not in seen:
            seen.add(m)
            result.append(m)
    return result

Flip the Matrix: Similar Movies

Everything we built compared people -- the columns of filled. But the same data read the other way compares movies: each row is a movie's vector of 15 ratings, and two movies whose rows point the same way are liked by the same people.

This powers the other famous recommendation sentence: "customers who watched this also watched..." -- no user profile needed at all.

Your task: repeat the Part 3 trick along the other axis:

  1. Scale each row of M = filled.values to length 1. Row lengths: np.sqrt((M ** 2).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) (the keepdims=True keeps the shape compatible so the division works row by row).
  2. S_items = uMr @ uMr.T -- note the transpose moved to the other side: entry (i, j) is now row-dot-row, movie i against movie j.
  3. Wrap it: msim = pd.DataFrame(S_items, index=filled.index, columns=filled.index).
  4. Write most_similar_movie(name) (mirror of most_similar).

What you invented: item-item collaborative filtering -- the variant Amazon famously chose, because with millions of users and thousands of products, item-item similarities are fewer, more stable, and reusable for every visitor.

Hint 1

Step 1: row_lengths = np.sqrt((M**2).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) then uMr = M / row_lengths.

Hint 2

Step 4: most_similar_movie works just like most_similar but uses msim instead of sim: msim[name].drop(name).idxmax().

Solution 
M = filled.values
row_lengths = np.sqrt((M**2).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
uMr = M / row_lengths
S_items = uMr @ uMr.T
msim = pd.DataFrame(S_items, index=filled.index, columns=filled.index)

def most_similar_movie(name):
    return msim[name].drop(name).idxmax()

Quick Check -- User-User vs Item-Item

You built two kinds of similarity: user-user (uM.T @ uM) and item-item (uMr @ uMr.T). If Netflix has 300 million users but only 20,000 movies, which approach produces a smaller, more manageable similarity table?

A. User-user, because users are more important than movies

B. Item-item, because a 20,000 x 20,000 table is much smaller than a 300-million x 300-million table -- and movie similarities change less often than user preferences

C. Both produce the same size table

D. Neither -- you need a completely different algorithm at that scale

Answer: B. A 20,000 x 20,000 item-item table has 400 million entries -- large but feasible. A 300M x 300M user-user table would have 90 quadrillion entries -- impossible to even store. Plus, movie taste profiles are more stable than individual user behavior, so the item-item table doesn't need constant recomputation.

Part 6: Scaling to Netflix -- MapReduce Matrix Multiplication

Our class matrix was 25 x 15. Netflix has around 300 million users and 20,000 titles. The user-similarity matrix alone would have $300{,}000{,}000 \times 300{,}000{,}000$ entries -- no single computer can even hold that, let alone compute it.

Two observations rescue us:

  1. The matrix is almost entirely zeros (it is "sparse"). A typical user rates a few dozen titles out of 20,000. Why store the zeros at all? Keep only the non-zero entries as (row, col, value) triples -- like a list of receipts instead of a massive spreadsheet with mostly blank cells.
  2. Matrix multiplication breaks down into tiny independent jobs. Recall: the result entry at row $i$, column $j$ is a sum of products. Each non-zero pair contributes one product to one output cell -- and every contribution can be computed on a different machine, then summed up per cell at the end. That "compute little pieces anywhere, then group and add by key" pattern is called MapReduce, and it's how the tech giants handle these enormous computations.

Sparse MapReduce Matrix Multiplication

Your task: write sparse_matmul(A_triples, B_triples) where each argument is a list of (row, col, value) triples representing the non-zero entries. Return a dict mapping (i, j) -> value for the non-zero entries of the product.

The key insight: for every non-zero entry A[i, k] and every non-zero entry B[k, j] that share the same middle index k, you get one contribution A[i,k] * B[k,j] to the output cell (i, j). Collect all such contributions and sum them per output cell.

Hint 1

First, group the B triples by their row index (the k value). A dictionary mapping k -> list of (j, value) makes lookups fast.

Hint 2

Loop over A triples. For each (i, k, a_val), look up all B triples with row k. For each (j, b_val) in that group, add a_val * b_val to your result dictionary at key (i, j).

Solution 
from collections import defaultdict

def sparse_matmul(A_triples, B_triples):
    # Group B by row
    B_by_row = defaultdict(list)
    for r, c, v in B_triples:
        B_by_row[r].append((c, v))

    result = defaultdict(float)
    for i, k, a_val in A_triples:
        for j, b_val in B_by_row[k]:
            result[(i, j)] += a_val * b_val
    return dict(result)

Part 7: What You Invented

This is collaborative filtering -- recommending purely from the pattern of who-likes-what, knowing nothing about the movies themselves (no genres, no actors, no plots). The alternative, content-based filtering, compares movie features instead; modern systems blend both.

And that uM.T @ uM trick -- all-pairs similarity as a single matrix product -- will meet you again in the most unexpected place: it's the heart of the attention mechanism inside large language models (the AI behind ChatGPT and similar tools), where every word in a sentence computes its similarity to every other word. Same math, different vectors.

uM.T @ uM (one matrix multiply for all pairs) All-pairs cosine via Gram matrix

Top-5 friends' top-5 favorites k-nearest-neighbors recommendation

You didn't learn recommender systems. You invented them.

Part 8: Reflection

Reflection

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. Why did we normalize before comparing? If you skipped the min-max scaling step, what kind of mistakes would the recommender make?
  2. User-user vs item-item: You built two approaches -- similarity between people and similarity between movies. When would you pick one over the other? Think about a system with many users but few products, versus one with few users but many products.
  3. The cold-start problem: A brand-new user with zero ratings can't get recommendations. Suggest two different strategies a real company might use to handle this.
  4. Beyond collaborative filtering: Our recommender knows nothing about the movies themselves -- no genres, no actors, no plot summaries. What problems might this cause? Can you think of a situation where two movies have very different content but get similar recommendations?
  5. The matrix multiplication trick: You computed all pairwise similarities in one line (uM.T @ uM). Why is this so much faster than a double for-loop calling similarity() for every pair?
